concept.name: Stream Watermarks & Late Data

relationships.description: Connects Stream Watermarks & Late Data to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Watermarks track event-time progress in unbounded streams, telling stateful operators when a time window is complete enough to emit results—while allowed lateness and side outputs handle straggling events.
spark.keyTakeaway: In Apache Flink or Spark Structured Streaming, set watermarks to max_observed_event_time - bounded_out_of_orderness, pair them with allowedLateness for corrections, and route beyond-lateness events to a side output rather than silently dropping them.

concept.whyItMatters: Mobile apps, IoT sensors, and multi-region Kafka topics deliver events out of order; without event-time watermarks, tumbling windows either emit wrong counts prematurely or hold state in memory forever until OOM.
whenToUse: Event-time aggregations (tumbling, sliding, or session windows) in Apache Flink, Apache Beam, or Spark Structured Streaming.
Out-of-order streams from mobile clients offline-buffering events, multi-AZ producers, or cross-region replication.
Billing, fraud detection, or SLA alerting where results depend on when an event occurred rather than when the server ingested it.
whenNotToUse: Simple stateless per-event transformations (filtering, JSON enrichment, regex masking) that require no windowing.
Strict processing-time monitoring where wall-clock ingestion rate is the actual metric (e.g., raw Kafka consumer lag).
Batch-only workloads over bounded, already-complete daily Parquet files.
keyPoints: Event time (when the action happened) differs from processing time (when the Flink/Spark worker sees the record); watermarks bridge the two.
A watermark W(t) is a monotonic assertion that no more events with timestamp <= t are expected; when W(t) passes window_end, the window fires.
Bounded-out-of-orderness watermarks (maxEventTime - delta) trade latency for completeness: larger delta catches more late events but delays window emission and increases state size.
An idle Kafka partition stops advancing its local watermark and stalls the global min-watermark across all parallel subtasks unless withIdleness() is configured.
Events arriving after W(t) passes window_end + allowedLateness are dropped from state—route them to a Dead Letter / side output for batch reconciliation.

examples.title: Flink 1.19 mobile telemetry 1-minute tumbling windows
examples.scenario: A ride-hailing app buffers GPS pings during tunnel drops; 99% arrive within 15 seconds, while 0.8% arrive up to 2 minutes late.
examples.outcome: Configuring WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(15)) with allowedLateness(Time.minutes(2)) and sideOutputLateData(lateTag) emits fast 15s-delayed dashboards, retracts/updates windows for stragglers, and logs < 0.2% ultra-late pings to S3.

examples.title: Stalled watermark from an idle regional Kafka partition
examples.scenario: A 16-partition Kafka topic has low overnight traffic on partition 12; Flink's operator watermark takes the minimum across all 16 partitions, freezing all window emissions for 4 hours.
examples.outcome: Adding .withIdleness(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) marks silent partitions as idle so active partitions continue advancing the global watermark smoothly.

tradeOffs.pro: A generous out-of-orderness bound (e.g., 60s) reduces late-data retractions and downstream upserts.
tradeOffs.con: Every window waits 60s longer to emit and retains open RocksDB/heap state for 60s more.

tradeOffs.factor: Allowed lateness vs. state storage cost
tradeOffs.pro: Keeping window state open for allowedLateness lets the stream engine emit accurate updated totals for late arrivals.
tradeOffs.con: RocksDB state size grows linearly with lateness duration, increasing checkpoint size and recovery time.

tradeOffs.pro: Emitting early speculative triggers plus late updates keeps dashboards fresh and eventually accurate.
tradeOffs.con: Downstream sinks must support idempotent upserts (e.g., PostgreSQL ON CONFLICT or ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree) rather than append-only logs.

failureModes.name: Idle partition watermark stall
failureModes.description: One empty or skewed Kafka partition emits no events, pinning the operator's min-watermark in the past and halting all window outputs while state grows unboundedly.
failureModes.mitigation: Always configure idle-source detection (withIdleness in Flink) and alert on watermark-to-wall-clock lag.

failureModes.name: Clock skew poisoning maxEventTime
failureModes.description: A single buggy client sends a timestamp 10 years in the future, jumping the watermark to 2036 and causing all real-time events to be treated as late and dropped.
failureModes.mitigation: Clamp or quarantine future timestamps (event_time > processing_time + max_skew) at the ingestion/deserialization boundary.

failureModes.name: Silent data loss on late records
failureModes.description: Default window operators silently discard records arriving after window_end + allowedLateness, causing revenue/billing undercounts.
failureModes.mitigation: Attach a side output (lateOutputTag) to route ultra-late records to a cold-path Parquet/S3 reconciliation job.

failureModes.name: Unbounded state on high-cardinality session windows
failureModes.description: Long allowedLateness combined with millions of per-user session keys exhausts RocksDB disk/memory and times out checkpoints.
failureModes.mitigation: Bound session gaps, set explicit State TTL, and size RocksDB block cache + incremental checkpoints.

commonMistakes: Assuming watermarks are global wall-clock timers rather than data-driven metadata flowing inside the stream.
Forgetting that an operator with multiple upstream inputs advances its watermark to min(input_watermarks), not max.
Leaving idle-partition timeouts unset on topics with uneven key distribution.
Using append-only sinks (like plain CSV or unkeyed Kafka) when allowedLateness emits multiple updates per window.
Trusting untrusted client device clocks without clamping future timestamps.

sections.content:
## The idea

In distributed streaming, network jitter and offline buffering scramble event arrival order. A **watermark** `W(t)` is a special timestamped marker injected into the data stream asserting that no further events with `event_time <= t` are expected. It decouples correctness (event time) from infrastructure speed (processing time), giving stateful operators a deterministic signal to fire windows and garbage-collect old state.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose we aggregate 1-minute tumbling windows (`[12:00, 12:01)`) with a 10-second out-of-orderness bound (`delta = 10s`) and `allowedLateness = 30s`:
1. Events with timestamps `12:00:15`, `12:00:48`, and `12:01:05` arrive. `maxEventTime` becomes `12:01:05`, so `W = 12:00:55` (window `[12:00, 12:01)` stays open).
2. Event `12:01:12` arrives -> `W = 12:01:02`. Because `W >= 12:01:00`, the `[12:00, 12:01)` window **fires** its initial aggregate.
3. Window state is **retained** until `W` reaches `12:01:30` (`window_end + allowedLateness`).
4. A late event `12:00:52` arrives while `W = 12:01:15`: it enters the retained window and triggers an **updated emission**.
5. Once `W >= 12:01:30`, the window state is **purged**; any subsequent `12:00:xx` event is routed to the **side output**.

data.caption: Watermarks advance window triggers monotonically while allowed lateness and side outputs prevent silent data loss on straggling records.

sections.content:
## Multi-partition and join alignment

Every parallel operator subtask tracks one watermark per input channel and sets its own watermark to the **minimum** across all active channels. This guarantees that a fast partition cannot prematurely close a window before a slower partition catches up. However, if a single partition goes silent, `withIdleness()` must mark it temporarily inactive so the minimum can advance. Similarly, in stream-stream interval joins, both sides buffer records in RocksDB until the combined minimum watermark passes the join upper bound.

## Late-data handling strategies

| Strategy | Latency | Completeness | State Cost | Downstream Requirement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Drop after Watermark** | Lowest | Drops stragglers > `delta` | Lowest | Append-only okay |
| **Allowed Lateness + Re-fire** | Low initial, eventual fix | High (covers `delta + lateness`) | Medium–High (RocksDB) | Idempotent upsert sink |
| **Side Output to Cold Path** | Low | 100% (via batch merge) | Low | Lambda/Kappa merge job |
| **Speculative Early Triggers** | Sub-second | Eventual | Medium | Upsert/retraction-aware sink |

## Failure modes

Two silent killers dominate production streaming: **clock-skew poisoning** (a single future-dated event jumps `W(t)` ahead by days, dropping all subsequent traffic as late) and **checkpoint backpressure** (when RocksDB state swells from long `allowedLateness`, checkpoint barriers stall behind full buffers, causing consumer lag to spiral).

## Monitoring watermark health

In Flink or Spark, monitor `currentInputWatermark` vs. wall-clock time (`watermarkLag = now - watermark`). A flatlining watermark while Kafka offsets climb indicates an idle partition or skewed key. Always expose a counter for `numLateRecordsDropped` and `sideOutputLateCount` so silent data loss triggers an alert immediately.

## Practical checklist

- Set `boundedOutOfOrderness` from the p99 arrival delay distribution, not a guess.
- Enable `withIdleness()` on all multi-partition Kafka sources.
- Clamp future client timestamps (`event_time > now + 5m`) before watermark assignment.
- Always attach a `sideOutputLateData` sink instead of silently dropping ultra-late records.
- Pair `allowedLateness` with an idempotent upsert sink (keyed by `window_start, key`).

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Stream Watermarks Late Data

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Watermarks track event-time progress in unbounded streams, telling stateful operators when a time window is complete enough to emit results—while allowed lateness and side outputs handle straggling events.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Window & State applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Primary & Side Sinks.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Primary & Side Sinks experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always configure idle-source detection (withIdleness in Flink) and alert on watermark-to-wall-clock lag.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: In Apache Flink or Spark Structured Streaming, set watermarks to max_observed_event_time - bounded_out_of_orderness, pair them with allowedLateness for corrections, and route beyond-lateness events to a side output rather than silently dropping them.
Avoid trap: Assuming watermarks are global wall-clock timers rather than data-driven metadata flowing inside the stream.
Avoid trap: Forgetting that an operator with multiple upstream inputs advances its watermark to min(input_watermarks), not max.
When to reach for it: Event-time aggregations (tumbling, sliding, or session windows) in Apache Flink, Apache Beam, or Spark Structured Streaming.
When to reach for it: Out-of-order streams from mobile clients offline-buffering events, multi-AZ producers, or cross-region replication.

putItTogether.outcome: Configuring WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(15)) with allowedLateness(Time.minutes(2)) and sideOutputLateData(lateTag) emits fast 15s-delayed dashboards, retracts/updates windows for stragglers, and logs < 0.2% ultra-late pings to S3.
